entries.label: VS Code
entries.description: The most versatile and well-supported development environment available. Microsoft's backing ensures long-term stability, extensive plugin ecosystem, and continuous improvement. Works seamlessly across languages and platforms.

entries.label: AWS CloudFormation
entries.description: Cloud-native IaC is the pragmatic default for single-cloud operations. CloudFormation (including CDK and Bicep for Azure) offers automatic state management, unified security model, 100% resource coverage, direct vendor support, and zero operational overhead. The 2024 IaC Generator eliminates brownfield migration challenges. Choose cloud-native unless you have specific cross-platform orchestration needs or genuine multi-cloud operations.

entries.label: Terraform
entries.description: Solid choice for cross-platform orchestration (AWS + GitHub + Datadog) and genuine multi-cloud operations. State management complexity and operational overhead are real costs—over 50% of users report state issues. OpenTofu fork addresses licensing concerns. Use when you need multi-tool coordination or have significant existing Terraform investment. For single-cloud infrastructure, cloud-native tools offer better long-term value.

entries.label: N8N
entries.description: Workflow automation platform with extensive integration capabilities. Interesting alternative to building custom async workers for internal processes and lower-volume workloads. Not suitable for high-throughput production systems, but compelling for operational workflows, internal tools, and personal automation.

entries.label: Domain-Driven Design
entries.description: My preferred approach for designing distributed systems. DDD doesn't force monolith vs. microservices decisions prematurely—bounded contexts let you discover boundaries and scale incrementally. Supports modular monoliths that can split when needed. Requires architectural governance but empowers teams to make detailed design decisions. Most effective for behavior-driven systems rather than pure entity-management scenarios.

entries.label: Test-Driven Development
entries.description: Essential practice for writing maintainable code. TDD encourages SOLID principles, user-focused design, and explicit testing of assumptions. Particularly valuable for developers building architectural discipline, but beneficial for all engineers. Forces consideration of use cases over isolated functions.

entries.label: Trunk-Based Development
entries.description: Critical for effective CI/CD. Enables faster feedback loops, eliminates work based on stale code, and significantly improves system stability. Teams committed to continuous delivery should adopt this practice.

entries.label: REST
entries.description: Still the right choice for entity-driven APIs—media libraries, inventory systems, configuration management. For business-logic-heavy operations, consider RPC-style APIs instead. Choose based on your domain characteristics, not trends.

entries.label: Behavior Driven Design
entries.description: Not recommended as a modern approach to high-quality development. Industry adoption is low and largely superficial; most teams using BDD tools like Cucumber or SpecFlow repurpose them for test automation rather than practicing genuine cross-functional behavior specification. The collaboration between business stakeholders and developers that BDD promises rarely materializes, Gherkin scenarios become a maintenance burden at scale, and well-structured TDD with integration tests delivers faster feedback with less ceremony. Shift-left testing and developer experience tooling have largely superseded BDD's value proposition.

entries.label: AWS
entries.description: Primary cloud platform choice based on service longevity and stability. AWS rarely deprecates services, protecting long-term architectural investments. Azure has superior billing management and DevOps tooling, making it attractive for smaller projects. Both are viable—choose based on organizational priorities and project requirements.

entries.label: Kubernetes
entries.description: Operational complexity and upgrade instability make K8s a difficult commitment. The overhead often outweighs benefits even for large microservice deployments. Carefully evaluate whether managed container services or serverless alternatives better serve your needs before adopting.

entries.label: Firebase
entries.description: Effective for rapid prototyping and initial launches, but limitations emerge quickly in production. Lacks built-in authorization (major gap), leading to accumulating technical debt. Good for MVPs, but plan migration path early if product gains traction.

entries.label: MySQL
entries.description: Reliable, performant, and universally supported relational database. Works well for service-based architectures that avoid heavy database scripting. PostgreSQL is equally solid. Despite being a .NET developer, I prefer MySQL over SQL Server for most use cases.

entries.label: Redis
entries.description: Avoid based on repeated operational failures across multiple organizations. Stability issues persist even with cloud-managed offerings. Identity crisis (cache? database? message broker?) leads to complex, fragile implementations. Modern cloud-native services solve the same problems more reliably.

entries.label: Memcached
entries.description: Stable, cost-effective caching solution. While clustering has limitations compared to cloud-native options, its simplicity and reliability make it superior to alternatives like Redis when used appropriately. Focus on caching use cases it handles well.

entries.label: DynamoDB
entries.description: Exceptional NoSQL database for the right use cases. Extremely fast, cost-effective, scales seamlessly, integrates perfectly with event-driven architectures. Works beautifully with bounded contexts and can replace entire architectural layers. Native caching support and change-stream capabilities enable real-time data pipelines.

entries.label: Clerk
entries.description: Full-stack authentication and user management platform with excellent UI SDK support. However, the data architecture is fundamentally flawed—built around single-app use cases with users siloed per application. Cross-app support exists through satellite domains, but this is a workaround for deeper architectural limitations. Great for rapid initial deployment (faster than Firebase or Supabase), but the solution reflects the same deployment-velocity mindset it promotes, lacking long-term architectural planning. Kinde offers similar features at lower cost with better multi-tenant flexibility, multi-domain support, and architectural alignment. While Clerk's SDK advantage is notable, AI-assisted form building eliminates this gap. Consider alternatives that provide better TCO, strategic flexibility, and mature multi-tenant architecture within the same cost range.

entries.label: Kinde
entries.description: Authentication and user management platform that hits the sweet spot among available solutions. Superior cost structure compared to Auth0 and Clerk, with better multi-tenant and branding support than Firebase, Supabase, or AWS Cognito. The data architecture is organization-oriented rather than app-centric, enabling true multi-tenant scenarios without architectural workarounds. Excellent UI console surpasses competing offerings in usability and feature completeness. Simple data migration paths and holistic approach to identity management across multiple applications and domains. While Auth0, Clerk, Firebase, Supabase, AWS Cognito, and WorkOS are all viable solutions for specific use cases, Kinde balances cost, architectural flexibility, enterprise features, and developer experience better than alternatives. Strong consideration for new projects requiring authentication with growth potential.

entries.label: TypeScript
entries.description: Compile-time safety reduces bugs and improves maintainability significantly. Rich tooling and type system help teams understand code better than relying solely on tests. Some verbosity exists for teams new to type safety, but the long-term benefits—fewer runtime errors, better refactoring, clearer contracts—outweigh learning curve.

entries.label: Vue
entries.description: Lightweight, performant framework with logical separation of concerns. Uses standard HTML without JSX abstraction (unlike React), while remaining flexible and unopinionated (unlike Angular). Smaller ecosystem than competitors but growing rapidly. Best balance of performance, developer experience, and pragmatic design.

entries.label: NUXT
entries.description: Full-stack Vue framework worth adopting if it fits your project's needs. Nuxt enforces a standardized project structure with conventions for routing, layouts, middleware, and state management, so teams spend less time debating folder organization and more time building features. The optional server engine (Nitro) provides a unified backend layer for API routes, server middleware, and data fetching without requiring a separate backend project, keeping the full stack in one codebase when that makes sense. Rendering flexibility is a major strength: SSR, SSG, ISR, SPA, and hybrid rendering modes are all available per-route, letting you optimize SEO-critical pages with server rendering while keeping interactive sections client-side. Under the hood, Vue's reactivity system and Nuxt's automatic code splitting, tree shaking, and lazy-loaded components deliver fast load times and smooth runtime performance. Auto-imports for composables, components, and utilities reduce boilerplate significantly. Version upgrades still require attention, and some abstractions over libraries like Tailwind can be limiting, but for projects that benefit from SSR, SEO, or a unified full-stack TypeScript experience, Nuxt delivers strong velocity with minimal configuration.

entries.label: Rust
entries.description: Impressive performance and safety guarantees, but significant investment in learning and team training. Better suited for systems programming, IoT, and critical async workflows than typical APIs. Not planning to use for most application development. Awaiting practical POC opportunity.

entries.label: GRPC
entries.description: High-performance RPC framework built on HTTP/2 with Protocol Buffers for strongly typed service contracts. gRPC excels at internal service-to-service communication where low latency and efficient binary serialization matter more than human-readable payloads. Contract-first development enforces clear API boundaries between services, and code generation from .proto files eliminates the drift between client and server that plagues REST-based integrations over time. Bidirectional streaming support opens patterns that REST simply cannot match, such as real-time feeds and long-lived connections. The tight coupling concern is real but manageable with proper bounded context design. Unlike WCF, gRPC is built on open standards with broad cross-language support, so the coupling is in the contract, not the platform. Currently evaluating in a POC to understand how it fits alongside event-driven and REST patterns in a distributed .NET architecture. The .NET implementation is first-class, with native integration into ASP.NET and excellent tooling in Aspire for local development.

entries.label: GraphQL
entries.description: Effective for internal tools and reporting dashboards. However, production experience revealed it often masks architectural and organizational problems rather than solving them. Modern team topologies (vertical slices, domain ownership) eliminate the API bottleneck GraphQL was meant to solve. Security, performance, and maintenance tradeoffs are significant. Use selectively.

entries.label: .NET
entries.description: Premier platform for enterprise systems. Mature, secure, well-supported ecosystem with excellent performance. While other languages may be simpler or have cleaner evolution paths, .NET strikes the best balance between technical capability and business velocity. Continuous innovation keeps it ahead of alternatives like Java.

entries.label: Jekyll
entries.description: Rock-solid static site generator backed by GitHub Pages. Perfect for content-heavy sites—blogs, documentation, portfolios—where dynamic features aren't needed. Simple architecture (Liquid templates, YAML front matter, Markdown content) makes it maintainable without framework churn. Native GitHub Pages integration means zero-config deployment. Compile-time rendering ensures exceptional performance and security. Great for technical writing where you want version control and simplicity over CMS complexity.

entries.label: .NET Aspire
entries.description: Should be the default starting point for any ASP.NET solution. The single biggest reason to adopt Aspire is the ability to test a fully distributed system on your local machine without provisioning remote environments. No shared dev clusters, no waiting on cloud deployments to validate integration behavior. You spin up the entire topology locally, including databases, caches, and message brokers, and test service interactions end-to-end before code ever leaves your machine. Even if you never deploy Aspire to production, this alone justifies adoption. Aspire orchestrates everything with a single F5 keystroke, eliminating Docker Compose files and manual startup scripts. The built-in dashboard gives you structured logging, distributed tracing, and metrics across all services out of the box, turning local debugging from guesswork into observability. Service discovery and connection string management are automatic, so adding a new dependency is a one-liner in your AppHost rather than configuration scattered across projects. Health checks, retry policies, and OpenTelemetry come wired in through opinionated defaults that follow production best practices. New team members spin up the full system in minutes instead of hours. For production, Aspire generates deployment manifests for Azure Container Apps, Kubernetes, or custom targets, but the real value is making distributed .NET development feel as simple as running a single project.

entries.label: .NET Blazor
entries.description: Blazor is a solid choice for self-contained, internal applications like admin dashboards, back-office tools, and ops consoles where user counts are bounded and the team is .NET-native. In that context, the single-language advantage is real: shared types, no npm dependency graph, and natural integration with ASP.NET authentication and middleware. Component libraries like MudBlazor and Radzen accelerate internal tool development significantly. However, Blazor Server's reliance on persistent SignalR connections creates a meaningful scaling constraint. Every connected user holds a WebSocket, requires server affinity, and consumes server-side memory for circuit state. This makes it a poor fit for public-facing or high-scale applications where horizontal scaling, CDN-friendly assets, and stateless request handling matter. Even for scenarios that genuinely need WebSocket communication, a dedicated API-layer solution like SignalR on ASP.NET or gRPC streaming offers better scalability without coupling the transport concern to the UI framework. WebAssembly mode addresses some scaling concerns but ships an entire .NET runtime to the browser, which introduces its own trade-offs around payload size and startup time. For enterprise web applications that need to scale, a decoupled architecture with Nuxt on the front end and .NET APIs on the back end provides better separation of concerns, independent scaling, and access to the full web platform without framework constraints. Blazor remains a strong recommendation for internal tooling where development velocity for .NET teams outweighs scaling considerations.
